errors.description: For a non-Archimedean place, χ_v(x,∞)=1/|x|_v makes the proximity contribution negative when x is divisible by the corresponding prime. This contradicts the stated counting formula (6) and prevents N(x,∞) from being the nonnegative count used later. For κ=Q, S={∞}, and x=p^k, the definition gives a contribution −k log p at p, while (6) gives an empty sum plus O(1).
errors.evidence: “If v is non-Archimedean, set … χ_v(x,a)=… 1/|x|_v : a=∞”; equation (6) sums only over v with ord_v(x⁻¹)>0.

errors.location: Proof of Theorem 1.4, paragraph beginning “By using Dirichlet's unit theorem”
errors.description: The asserted uniform comparison between the absolute values of an algebraic integer at all Archimedean places is false, even for units. In Q(√2), powers of 1+√2 have embedding absolute values whose ratio grows without bound. Thus the claimed O(1) bound for m(y,0) does not follow; for those powers, the contribution from the embedding of absolute value √2−1 grows linearly with the exponent.
errors.evidence: “there exists a constant c(κ) such that |y|_v ≤ c(κ)|y|_w for any Archimedean v, w”; the proof then concludes “m(y,0)=…=O(1).”

errors.location: Theorem 2.1 statement and its construction of x′; Proof of Theorem 1.5
errors.description: Theorem 2.1 requires a single x′ that works for all but finitely many x, but the subsequent construction chooses ideals from the prime factorization of x and x−a_j, so the resulting x′ depends on x. This matters in Theorem 1.5: for κ=Q, a₁=0, a₂=1, and simple x=1/p, the claimed y=(x−a₁)(x−a₂)/x′ cannot be integral for all sufficiently large primes p if x′ is fixed, since its denominator contains p² and a fixed rational x′ can cancel only finitely many such primes.
errors.evidence: Theorem 2.1: “There exist an extension field K … and an element x′∈K such that all but finitely many x∈κ”; the later construction defines ideals using “(x)” and “(x−a_j)”; Theorem 1.5 asserts “y=1/(x′Q(x)) is an algebraic integer.”

errors.description: The proof uses the wrong sign and therefore applies Theorem 1.5 at the wrong second finite point. Under the stated relation a+b=c and x=a/c, the second point is 1 because x−1=−b/c; the proof instead uses −1 and then identifies x+1 with b/c. Its separate assertion a+b+c=0 also conflicts with the theorem's stated equation.
errors.evidence: Theorem 1.6 assumes “a+b=c”; the proof says “Since a+b+c=0” and applies (12) at x=a/c with points 0 and −1, then equates the −1 count to the primes dividing b.
